children: Artificial intelligence is swallowing an unprecedented share of U.S. venture capital, but Social Capital founder Chamath Palihapitiya is warning that the quality of the revenue supporting that boom may deserve much closer scrutiny.
AI and machine-learning companies accounted for roughly
83% of U.S. venture capital deal value through September 2026
, according to data shared by Social Capital.
That is up sharply from
, and it represents the highest share shown in the firm's historical data.
The shift has been dramatic.
AI accounted for only about
10% of U.S. venture deal value in 2015
, before rising to 26% in 2020, 31% in 2021 and 2022, 39% in 2023, 51% in 2024 and 65% last year.
Now, more than four out of every five venture dollars are flowing into AI-related companies.
But Palihapitiya argues that headline growth may not tell the full story.
He said he suspects that roughly
70% to 80% of AI-company revenue comes from other AI companies that themselves raised money from venture capital investors
The issue, in his view, is not necessarily circular revenue by itself.
It is whether that revenue reflects durable end-market demand or a funding ecosystem where venture-backed companies increasingly sell products and services to one another.
Palihapitiya compared the dynamic with patterns he says emerged during the software-as-a-service boom in the early and mid-2010s.
Investor Takeaway
I think the 83% figure is striking for two reasons.
First, it shows just how concentrated venture investing has become around one theme.
Second, Chamath's criticism raises an important question about whether some of the AI economy is being supported by
capital flowing from investors into startups, then from one startup into another
That does not automatically mean the revenue is low quality.
AI infrastructure providers can generate perfectly legitimate revenue from other AI companies.
The real test is what happens if fundraising slows.

If customers can continue paying for compute, models and software from internally generated cash flow, the revenue becomes much more durable. If spending depends heavily on repeated venture rounds, growth could prove more fragile.
For investors, the key things to watch are
customer concentration, cash burn, outside-enterprise adoption, free cash flow and how much AI revenue ultimately comes from customers outside the venture-funded ecosystem

title: Billionaire Investor Flags a Troubling Twist in AI Boom
